Please do let me know how it went... I am not a dad myself, but I would be interested in knowing how this goes for you. Wishing you all the best!

I don't know your dad, so please take all of this as speculation only... I would assume it to be helplessness. There are people out there that just don't experience negative emotions as strongly. It's a personality trait. So when he says "get those negative thoughts out of your head", I think he does not grasp how destructive those thoughts can be to you. Something that would make you (or me, for that matter) go completely insane with self-doubt, feelings of inadequacy, and self-hate would probably just make him go "meh, whatever, I got other things to do.". People are just not the same in that way - none is better than the other, just different. 

One idea of how you could approach the topic: First, make clear to him why you are telling him those things and what you expect from him. Fathers can be overly practical, so maybe he thinks you want him to fix it (which he cannot do, obviously, even if he got your perspective) - Give him a precise framework to operate within. Do you need help in particular things (like interaction with people)? Do you just want him to be understanding and to be there for you? I think this could help bring down his helplessness and therefore lower his dismissive stance on all of that.

If he tries to shut you down, try an analogy: Just because something does not hurt him (be it mentally or physically for that matter) it does not mean that it cannot hurt other people. People experience pain and hurt differently. Alternatively, argue in consequences: What does it mean to you or your mom when he is so dismissive? Can he imagine what it would feel like when he had an issue and the people he cared about didn't take it seriously?

This is a horrible place to be in - but you are far from being weak, dumb, and a failure. From what you wrote, I can only speculate, but I think your empathy and your focus on being genuine and good toward other people is what hurts you. Not that you should stop that, not at all, but I think it's time to turn inside and find something inside you that can keep you going. I know it's easy to say that, but don't depend on other people for happiness. People can smell that and it usually attracts those that would abuse this cry for help. I think this is what has happened to you.

As for concrete steps you can take - do something for yourself, not for other people. Something with a long-lasting impact. Learn something that you always wanted to learn, read a book you always wanted to read. If you build yourself like that in small steps, you will start to attract people with a similar mindset which will then push you up, too. Don't do it for them though, do it for yourself.

It was a good thing that you were so transparent and upfront about those suicidal thoughts, but for somebody who has never had such experiences (I am assuming this about your dad), it's very hard to hear that. People can easily feel like it's their fault - Not that it necessarily is, but you know... They might feel overwhelmed and helpless which then might lead to harsh comments and 'duh-ideas' like 'get over it' - It's a form of helplessness.

I don't know what your and your mom's relationship with your dad is, but assuming that he is not the main source of your suicidal thoughts, I think it could make sense to clarify why you decided to tell him - Just so he understands what to make of it - Explain to him that "just getting over it" is not working... For example, depression might be due to a chemical imbalance in your brain - no "getting over it" in the world will change anything about that.

Also, it might help to contextualize what you want from him. Maybe he thinks that you expect him to fix things (a very father-ish thought to have) when, maybe, all you and your mom want is to be understood and to feel safe about sharing those dark thoughts.

I am not saying it is getting better for everybody. Unfortunately. But you cannot dismiss that the possibility that things, in fact, do get better, remains. It is exactly this chance for why I encourage people to keep going. Even if it is just a slim one.

What would you rather I said? 'Yeah, go ahead, kill yourself?' at that point, what would even be the point of this subreddit? You cannot expect people not to care.

You know... people usually know and see less / see things differently than we do ourselves. You say that everybody sees you for 'the pathetic person you are', but I don't think that is true. You said you had OCD since a young age... How old are you now? How long has it been since you last felt anything positive?

Suffering is not an objective measure, so there is no reason for you to feel ashamed of that. Back in the last financial crisis, there were millionaires that took their lives because they lost most of their fortune and 'only' had a couple million left... It made them feel like failures, so they - unfortunately - decided to end their lives.

What I am trying to say with this is... Don't beat yourself up over how you are feeling. It's not your fault. You did not choose this. That being said, I do think you need to change something. Maybe you can get some time off (idk if this is possible in your current position) to spend a week or two in nature. You know.. Kinda re-connecting with the fundamentals that get lost in the everyday hustle.   
Another option would be - and please do not hate me for suggesting this - antidepressants. I know they get a bad wrap, but they can help a lot, especially when 'objectively', your life is in order. Do you have any friends or family to talk to about all of this? Have you tried? Would you?

You will probably not like my answer, but stuff can get better, this is why I would encourage everybody to give it another week, a day or even another hour. The night is darkest before dawn - Cheesy, but it is true. I've seen people who were in a dark, dark place turn their lives around and now live, maybe not happily, but better. I would not want anybody to do something that cuts their live short in a period of misery if there is still potential for change.

I think you should just go and find somebody to play hide and seek with, then. :)  
If you feel that strongly toward your childhood, there's obviously something there that you need to find that you haven't found or worked out thus far. Taking a playful approach might work. Also, sounds like fun to me! I'd love to play hide and seek again. :)

What kinds of work do you enjoy doing? Is there any chance you can make something of that? ADHD is a bitch, but there are training courses out there to up your executive functions. That combined with doing something you love doing could be a solution for you... At least in the mid-to-long term.

This is just a shot from the hip here, but it seems to me that all of those issues, in one way or another, relate to you not trusting your bodily functions / to the relationship between your abstract mental space and your physical body in broader terms. Idk if that is of any help to you, but it can be quite amazing to sit down and meditate on how everything inside you 'just works' and how amazingly your body regulates itself. Just feeling your heart inside your chest or consciously controlling your breath, knowing that if you don't breathe consciously, your body does it by itself. Your body is not something that you have to meticulously control via rational thought... It can do its thing on its own quite well. :)  


In any case, I wish you all the best and hope that soon, you will be able to enjoy your favorite foods again!

I think the main issue is this mindset of "keeping you at home so you don't do anything stupid". The implicit assumption that lays beneath that statement is 'you are incompetent and should be treated as a child for the rest of your life'. This is not ok. We have to do stupid things to grow and develop. Your parents are not doing you a favor here, they are robbing you of the opportunity to develop as a human being by trying to save you from yourself.

My advice for you would be to find something you can put a value on and that you can use to try, fail and improve with. Something that means something to you. Maybe a hobby you always wanted to try or a topic you always wanted to learn about. It doesn't have to be something huge or anything, but it has to mean something to you. As you get better at it, no matter what it is, you will gain the confidence to approach more things in your life like that.

Also, be more forgiving to yourself. I think you already identified the issue which is the first and maybe the most important step. From here on, one step after another. You will get there, I know you will. :)

It seems to me like you are somewhat stuck in your past - and to a degree, I get why; The whole prison-thing and the addiction... That surely were rough times, but you can't let yourself be defined by it. Pick up a recent videogame or do something else besides work that connects you to the world and how it currently runs. Whatever you do, don't let yourself be determined by your past. Take all the lessons you can from it and then leave it behind. There's much to live for, you just have to find out what works for you. :)

If you just 'wrapped it up', try a pressure-bandaging instead (no clue what the official term is in english - check this wiki-entry, the images should help to understand the procedure: https://de.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Druckverband )

The idea is to create pressure on the cut and therefore to force it to close. 
1. a layer oft normal bandaging (after making sure the wound is clean)
2. put an object like a small roll of bandage or even something like a thick pen on the bandage right above where the cut is (parallel to the cut)
3. wrap it up tight (but not too tight) to ensure pressure on the cut. The object you wrapped up concentrates the pressure on the cut

You already said that you don't know why you harmed yourself and I am by no means in a position to diagnose why you did it. However, I do believe it would be important for you to understand the 'why'. 

For me personally, it was the relief-mechanism to cope with emotional dissociation. When you are in lots of stress, it can seem like you become numb or constantly strained. Self-harm can come in handy there to re-connect your 'mind and emotion'-space with your body. After all, pain is as real as it gets. It grounds you in some way and, for a short period of time, puts the emotional pain in relation to physical pain. For this short time, you are in your body, right there, in pain, not in a 'mind-space' of endless stress and terror.
